newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Jan 30.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Jan 30.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- HOPES RISE FOR 'OPEN SKIES' AGREEMENT

American sources indicate that an agreement is 90 percent complete for the creation of a new transatlantic air pact to pave the way for approval of the British Airways alliance with American Airlines. The two airlines may have to push back implementation from April to the end of the year due to delays in gaining regulatory clearance. Transport Secretary George Young is understood to have bowed to American pressure to allow UK carriers to use Heathrow as a staging post to fly on to other destinations but is reluctant to make similar concessions for cargo flights.
-- 150,000 SAVERS IGNORE A REMINDER WORTH 250 STG

Bristol and West's advice has been ignored by more than 150,000 savers, who have done themselves out of 250 stg in bonuses payable on its takeover by the Bank of Ireland. Bristol and West told savers who had less than 100 stg in their accounts that they must make sure they brought their balances up to 100 stg by December 31 if they wanted to get the bonuses. Some 70 percent of low-balance savers did not top up their accounts.
-- REPOSSESSIONS AT LOWEST SINCE 1989

According to the Council of Mortgage Lenders, home repossessions last year, at more than 800 a week, were their lowest since 1989. Director general, Michael Coogan, said that the large fall in mortgage arrears and possessions in the second half of 1996 is beyond expectations. However, mortgage lenders remain aware that arrears and possession levels are still well above those of the 1980s.
THE TIMES
-- AVOIDANCE COSTS TWO BILLION STG IN VAT

The National Audit Office annual report on the accounts of HM Customs and Excise shows there is an embarrassing gulf between the expected and actual receipts. The report suggests that wily accountants were responsible for the five billion stg shortfall in VAT receipts last year. The National Lottery affected income by diverting money away from goods subject to VAT, and cost 260 million stg in lost revenue.
-- MARKS AND SPENCER SALES IMPROVE THANKS TO HOME HELP

Marks and Spencer, the high street company, have revealed that sales of its home furnishings division, Homeware, have surged 34 percent during the winter, due to the stronger housing market. A spokesman said that the new home furnishings catalogue has been selling well. M&S confirmed that peak sale of food, which rose 4.9 percent in the five weeks to January 4, arrived later in December than usual.
-- CITY ANGER OVER FARNELL WARNING

Anglo-American components group, Premier Farnell, has put out a profits warning less than a year after Farnell Electronics gained approval for its controversial 1.85 billion stg purchase of US group Premier. Profits for the year would be eight percent below market expectations at 135 million stg. The group blamed weak markets in the US and UK, along with the strong pound. The City is very unhappy because the group was due to give a series of analysts briefings on current trading yesterday, but cancelled them at the last minute.
THE GUARDIAN
-- CBI SPIKES ANTI-UNION POLICY

Plans, outlined in a green paper, by the Conservative Party to outlaw strikes have been rejected by the CBI as unworkable and likely to make industrial relations worse. The CBI's governing council warned the proposals would have a "disproportionate" or "excessive" impact and they would be unlikely to resolve disputes and could "lead to more uncertainty in the workplace". This follows consultation with the CBI's member firms and was seized on by Labour and the TUC as further proof that business is in the process of distancing itself from the Tories in advance of a change of government.
-- TWO CHEERS FOR WH SMITH'S SALES GROWTH

WH Smith have seen a three percent sales growth in December, however, new chief executive, Bill Cockburn, warned that it had completed only the first year of a four-year recovery programme. Shares in the group rose by five and a half pence to 430 pence. Profits bounced back after last year's troubles to 39 million stg, more than double last year's 17 million stg. The increase has stemmed from Cockburn's reorganisation measures, such as the sale of loss-making businesses.
-- GUMMER URGES MORE RECYCLING

Regulations, published by Environment Secretary, John Gummer, requiring businesses to meet recovery targets, urges consumers to buy more recycled products and support local collection schemes for used packaging. The new rules will not boost kerbside collections of domestic waste for several years and were criticised by environmental lobby group Friends of the Earth as unambitious. The rules aim to meet the requirement of a European Directive demanding that Britain improve its 27 percent recycling rate.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- FORD'S PLANTS IN EUROPE PLUNGE 180 MILLION STG INTO THE RED

US car giant Ford Motor Co has admitted that its European operations have plunged into the red due to falling demand, intense competition and huge overcapacity. The group reported losses of $291 million in 1996, compared with profits of $116 million in 1995. Figures suggest losses from Ford's British subsidiary have worsened considerably. Also, Ford's unions have succeeded in having time allocated for a Parliamentary debate on the company's plans to cut 1,300 jobs at
Halewood.
-- GRADE RULES OUT EARLY LEISURE ACQUISITIONS

Michael Grade, former chief executive of Channel Four, has confirmed he will become chief executive of First Leisure, the leisure group. He has ruled out an acquisition of Rank's film distribution arm and refused to cast any light on his ambitions for the group, however, he promised a continuation of the company's low profile strategy. He is replacing John Conlan.
-- BANK WARNS RATES NEED TO RISE SHARPLY

Governor of the Bank of England, Eddie George, has warned Chancellor Kenneth Clarke that interest rates would have to rise more sharply in the new year if he did not increase the cost of borrowing straight away. His forthright approach has revealed the split between himself and the Chancellor is wider than previously expected. City experts believe the Bank would advise Clarke to increase the cost of borrowing after the next monetary meeting, even though recent figures have given the Chancellor
more ammunition to resist.
